insider_note: The integral of v/(1 − 2v²) is not a plain log form until a −4 is forced into the numerator to match the derivative of the denominator — spot that adjustment early instead of guessing the antiderivative.

steps.label: Recognise homogeneous form and substitute
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Both terms on the right have total degree 2, so the ratio v = y/x is the right substitution.
steps.memory_tip: Homogeneous of degree 2 over degree 1 (after clearing x) still reduces to a function of v alone — check the RATIO, not each term separately.
lines: Given D.E is (x² − y²)dx − xy dy = 0
Put y = vx ⇒ dy/dx = v + x·dv/dx
steps.why: Rewriting the equation as dy/dx = (a function of x and y that only depends on the ratio y/x) confirms it is homogeneous, and the y = vx substitution turns it into an equation for v alone.
common_mistakes: Writing xy dy = (x² − y²)dx with a sign error, flipping the original equation.
Simplifying (x² − v²x²)/(x·vx) incorrectly and losing the x²/x² cancellation.

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Subtract v from both sides before separating.
steps.memory_tip: Combine (1 − v²)/v − v over the common denominator v.
steps.why: Subtracting v as a single fraction over v combines the two terms into one clean function of v, which is what makes the equation separable.
common_mistakes: Writing (1 − v²)/v − v as (1 − v² − v)/v instead of correctly combining v = v²/v.
Losing the factor of 2 in front of v² when combining terms.

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Force a −4v into the numerator to match the derivative of (1 − 2v²), then correct with a compensating factor of −1/4.
steps.memory_tip: The derivative of 1 − 2v² is −4v, so v dv needs a −1/4 out front to become that exact log-integral shape.
steps.why: The derivative of the denominator 1 − 2v² is −4v, so writing the numerator as −4v times −1/4 turns the left integral into a direct log form, matching the ∫dx/x = log x on the right.
common_mistakes: Integrating v/(1 − 2v²) as if it were already in the form f′(v)/f(v), without the −1/4 correction factor.
Dropping the constant of integration on one side only.

steps.label: Return to x and y
steps.margin_note: One mark. Multiply the log equation by −4 to clear the fraction before substituting v = y/x.
steps.memory_tip: Multiplying by −4 turns log(cx) into log(cx)⁻⁴ = log(1/(cx)⁴) on the right.
steps.why: Multiplying both sides of the log equation by −4 removes the fraction, and only then is it clean to substitute v = y/x, since the −4 power would otherwise complicate the fraction further.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to flip the sign when multiplying an equation by a negative number.
Substituting v = y/x before clearing the −4 power, producing a much messier line.

steps.label: Final equation
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Cross-multiply and relabel the arbitrary constant. The constant c⁴ is renamed c on the last line — an arbitrary positive constant raised to a fixed power is still an arbitrary constant.
steps.memory_tip: Since c is arbitrary throughout, cx⁴(x² − 2y²) = x² can be rewritten as x²(x² − 2y²) = c by renaming 1/c as c.
steps.why: Cross-multiplying clears the last fraction, and because c was an arbitrary constant from the start, relabelling 1/c as a new c keeps the final relation in its simplest whole form.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as cx²(x² − 2y²) = 1 instead of relabelling the constant.
Losing a factor of x² when cross-multiplying.
